headline: Malaysia caps its debt at 65%; the bigger pension bill has no ceiling
context: Fiscal debate fixes on the 65% statutory debt ceiling. The civil-service pension bill, projected at RM42.8 billion in 2026 and rising toward RM120 billion a year by 2040, sits outside that ceiling and outside any cap, paid each year from current revenue.

cards.big: Malaysia argues over a 65% debt ceiling. The civil-service pension bill, heading for RM120 billion a year, answers to no ceiling at all.
cards.sub: Pensions are a promise to nearly a million retirees, paid from each year's revenue, and counted against no cap.

cards.big: The 2026 pension bill is set at RM42.8 billion, the fourth-largest item in federal spending, up from about RM11 billion in 2010.
cards.sub: On the government's own projection it reaches roughly RM120 billion a year by 2040.

cards.big: The debt everyone watches is capped at 65% of GDP. The pension promise behind it, put between RM483 billion and RM1.3 trillion, has no cap and no fund.
cards.sub: No single audited figure exists; the estimates range that far because the liability was never fully provisioned.

cards.big: In 2022 about eight working-age Malaysians stood behind each person over 65. By 2040 it is fewer than five.
cards.sub: And 3.45 million informal workers will reach old age largely outside the EPF, the savings system meant to catch them.

cards.big: The ceiling caps the debt that is easy to count. The pension promise is harder to count, impossible to recall, and far larger.
Like watching the credit-card limit while a far larger mortgage, signed decades ago, falls due a little more every year.
A pension is an amanah: promised in good faith, owed in full. The honest question is not whether to pay it, but whether a shrinking workforce ever agreed to fund it.
